o: We maintain a set of uploaded videos and must answer, at any time, the largest $i$ such that videos $1..i$ are all uploaded. In the example: after uploading 3 the answer is 0 (video 1 missing); after uploading 1 it is 1; after uploading 2 it becomes 3. Since each video is uploaded exactly once and queries interleave with updates, we need a data structure supporting 'mark video v' and 'longest prefix of marks starting at 1' efficiently. With n up to 1e5 and 2e5 calls total, an amortized O(1) pointer or O(log n) per operation structure both work easily.
k: The longest uploaded prefix can only move forward over time, since uploads are never removed.
A single pointer that advances while the next video is already uploaded gives amortized O(n) total work across all operations.
Equivalently, a max-heap or union-find can track which prefixes are complete, but the simple pointer is optimal.

a.n: Approach 1: Boolean array + brute-force scan from 1
a.i: Mark uploads in a boolean array; for each longest() call scan from video 1 upward until a gap is found. This is the most direct translation of the definition. It passes constraints only because the number of calls is bounded, but repeated scans are wasteful when many longest() calls occur.
s: Keep boolean array seen[1..n] initialized to false.
longest(): start i = 1, advance while seen[i], return i - 1.
a.t: O(n) per longest() call in the worst case, O(n) total for uploads — acceptable given ≤2e5 calls but not optimal if longest() is called many times on a long prefix.

a.i: Since uploads never disappear, the longest prefix length is non-decreasing. Keep a persistent pointer that starts at 0; whenever we query, advance it as long as video pointer+1 has been uploaded. Each video causes the pointer to move at most once, so total pointer movement across all calls is O(n), giving amortized O(1) per operation.
s: Store uploads in a boolean array and initialize pointer p = 0.
longest(): while seen[p+1] is true, increment p.
Return p. The pointer never moves backward, so total advancement is at most n.
a.t: Amortized O(1) per operation — the pointer advances at most n times total across the whole run, and upload is O(1).

a.i: Push every uploaded video into a min-heap; the longest prefix equals the count of consecutive smallest elements 1, 2, ... popped from the heap top. Alternatively, union-find with path compression merges each uploaded video with its neighbor so that find(1)-style roots track contiguous blocks. Both give O(log n) or near-O(1) amortized behavior, but add complexity without beating the monotonic pointer.
s: Use a min-heap of uploaded videos plus a counter ans = 0.
upload(v): push v onto the heap.
longest(): while heap is non-empty and heap top == ans + 1, pop and increment ans.
a.t: O(log n) per upload (heap push); longest() is amortized O(log n) since each video is popped once overall.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 2: the observation that the prefix length is monotonically non-decreasing makes a single forward-moving pointer the cleanest O(1) amortized solution — mention Approach 3 to show awareness of alternatives (heap/union-find/BIT/segment tree all solve it, but are overkill here). Pitfalls: forgetting the empty-prefix case (answer 0 before video 1 arrives), allocating arrays of size n+1 vs n+2 (off-by-one when checking p+1), and assuming longest() needs a full rescan instead of caching state. Edge cases: uploading videos out of order, calling longest() before any upload, and n=1. Follow-ups might ask for dynamic removals (then a segment tree/BIT or ordered set is needed) or streaming with limited memory (bitset compression).
